changes.title: Rules library 1.5.0: every extra rule now rests on an official source
changes.summary: Seven state-specific extra rules in Colorado, Kansas, Louisiana (two), Nevada, New Jersey and Tennessee were re-read at the official source and now carry the exact quote. Louisiana's drug-ad statute is cited at its current number, Revised Statutes 51:3251, and its line and Kansas's now say who the law reaches. Five market notes that rested on a non-official source were taken out of the library.

source.label: Louisiana R.S. 51:3251

changes.title: Arkansas: six rule cells now state Arkansas’s own rules
changes.summary: The Arkansas cells on filing, required content, waiting periods, claims, referral payments and other languages now state the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct, Rules 7.1 to 7.5 (rule current to June 12, 2025), each with the words quoted from the Arkansas Judiciary’s page, in place of the ABA Model Rule default. The cells add a 30-day wait on written solicitation in death claims, a five-year record of each ad, and limits on testimonials, clients and dramatization in ads. The privacy cell now says only what the Attorney General’s page says.

source.label: Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct (Arkansas Judiciary)

changes.title: Massachusetts: Rule 7.3 comment [6] restated
changes.summary: Comment [6] says a person undergoing active medical treatment for traumatic injury is unlikely to be in an emotional state in which reasonable judgment about employing a lawyer can be exercised; the cell now states it that way.

source.label: Massachusetts Rule 7.3 comment [6]

changes.title: District of Columbia: 21-day statute added
changes.summary: District of Columbia Code § 22-3225.14 bars a practitioner from soliciting a client for financial gain within 21 days of a motor vehicle accident, with listed exceptions; the waiting-period cell and the state list now include it.

changes.title: Georgia: HB 1344 replaces the runner statute
changes.summary: HB 1344 (2026) repeals O.C.G.A. §33-24-53 effective January 1, 2027 and adds §33-1-9.2, with a felony penalty of up to ten years in prison and a fine up to $200,000 per violation.

source.label: Georgia HB 1344 (2026), as signed

changes.title: Alabama: do-not-call damages added
changes.summary: Alabama Code § 8-19C-7 also lets the person recover actual monetary loss from a knowing violation or up to $2,000 in damages for each knowing violation, whichever is greater; the cell now says so.

source.label: Code of Alabama § 8-19C-7

changes.title: California: Section 2874 route added
changes.summary: Public Utilities Code § 2873 allows automatic dialing-announcing calls under a prior agreement or as Section 2874 specifies; the cell now names both.

source.label: California Public Utilities Code § 2873

changes.title: Missouri: patent and admiralty exceptions added
changes.summary: Rule 4-7.4 excepts patent and admiralty designations from the specialist disclaimer; the cell now says so.

source.label: Missouri Rule 4-7.4

changes.title: District of Columbia: Opinion 342 note restated
changes.summary: Opinion 342 concludes that a flat fee for transmittals, or for each client secured, violates neither District of Columbia Rule 7.1 nor Rule 5.4; the note now states that conclusion only.

source.label: D.C. Bar Legal Ethics Committee, Opinion 342

changes.title: Maryland: keyword opinion comparison restated
changes.summary: Ethics Docket 2022-02 contrasts Texas Opinion 661, which found no violation, and New Jersey Opinion 735, which found no violation in buying the name alone; the note now names those opinions.

source.label: Maryland State Bar Association, Ethics Docket No. 2022-02

changes.title: Michigan: opinion on percentage marketing fees added
changes.summary: The Michigan page now carries State Bar of Michigan Opinion R-25 (July 27, 2018): a for-profit online matching service that holds the lawyer's fee and takes a percentage of it is an improper referral service and fee split. No coded value changed.

source.label: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics, R-25 (2018-07-27)

changes.title: Illinois: opinion on paying marketing companies added
changes.summary: The Illinois page now carries ISBA Opinion 06-02 (July 2006, affirmed January 2010): a firm may not pay a marketing company based on fees from clients it sends. The page shows it alongside Rule 7.2 as rewritten effective July 1, 2025. No coded value changed.

source.label: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions, 06-02 (2006-07)

changes.title: Oregon: chatbot opinion added to the state page
changes.summary: The Oregon page now carries Formal Opinion 2026-208 (February 2026): lawyers may use chatbots and AI agents for marketing and intake if they vet the tool and its vendors, can monitor and correct its answers, and supervise its work. No coded value changed.

source.label: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee), 2026-208 (2026-02)

changes.title: South Carolina: opinion on nonlawyer-owned firms added
changes.summary: The South Carolina page now carries Ethics Advisory Opinion 25-02 (2025): a lawyer may not serve as local co-counsel with, or own part of, an alternative business structure that has nonlawyer owners or pays nonlawyers who refer clients. No coded value changed.

source.label: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee, 25-02 (2025)

changes.title: Rhode Island: court's AI guidelines added
changes.summary: The Rhode Island page now carries the Supreme Court's interim generative AI guidelines (advisory, adopted June 17, 2026): a website chatbot does not lessen a lawyer's duties to people seeking a lawyer, and the lawyer remains responsible for AI-made ads. No coded value changed.

source.label: Rhode Island Supreme Court, Interim Guidelines for the Ethical Use of Generative AI by Rhode Island Lawyers

changes.title: Utah: referral fees prohibited
changes.summary: Utah Rule 5.4(c), which says referral fees are prohibited, took effect on November 1, 2026. Fee sharing with a lawyer is now allowed only under the new Rule 5.8.

source.label: Utah Rule 3-5.4

changes.title: Drug and device ad laws: the federal baseline added
changes.summary: The library's section on laws about ads for prescription drugs and medical devices now opens with the federal baseline that applies in every state, the FTC Act's ban on unfair or deceptive acts or practices and the FTC's letters on television ads for drug lawsuits, quoted from the official sources, before the states that have a law of their own. The data file and the page now carry that baseline and the state laws, each quoted with its sources.

source.label: FTC press release, Sept. 24, 2019: FTC Flags Potentially Unlawful TV Ads for Prescription Drug Lawsuits

changes.title: Rules library 1.3.0: every rule re-read at the official source
changes.summary: Version 1.3.0 of the rules library (October 28, 2026) re-read every rule cell at the state's official source (high court or official bar rules, official ethics opinions, official code sites) and added the words quoted from each source. No cell cites a legal-marketing firm, law firm blog or tracker any more: all published rules cite the official source. Coded values that changed: Delaware and Nevada recording (now mixed), Michigan and Utah waiting periods (30 days), Mississippi's set notice in every ad, Maryland's filing of targeted solicitations, New Jersey's required content and Vermont's health-data law. Also adds state laws on drug and medical-device ads and a federal consent note for web-form leads.

source.label: Probative lawyer advertising rules dataset, version 1.3.0 (all cells, sources and quotes)

changes.title: Rules library update: Kentucky and Maryland source links
changes.summary: Version 1.1.1 of the rules library (October 27, 2026) updated the source links and accessed dates for the Kentucky and Maryland ad-filing cells. No rule text changed.

source.label: Zenodo record of the Probative lawyer advertising rules dataset, version 1.1.1

changes.title: Rules library update: entries changed from state sources
changes.summary: Version 1.1.0 of the rules library (October 26, 2026) updated rule cells after a primary-source change.

source.label: Zenodo record of the Probative lawyer advertising rules dataset, version 1.1.0

changes.title: Rhode Island does have an ad copy-filing rule
changes.summary: Our library said Rhode Island had no filing rule, but Rule 7.2(b) says a copy of each print, radio and TV ad goes to Supreme Court Disciplinary Counsel before or within 48 hours of first use.

source.label: R.I. Rules of Professional Conduct 7.2(b)

changes.title: Nevada no longer has a 4-year ad-copy period
changes.summary: We had listed a 4-year period for keeping copies of ads in Nevada, but the current Rule 7.2, amended in 2018, has no such clause.

source.label: Nevada Rules of Professional Conduct 7.2 and 7.2A

changes.title: Kansas: ad-copy keeping period added
changes.summary: Kansas lawyers must keep a copy of each ad for 2 years after its last use (KRPC 7.2(b)); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Kansas KRPC 7.2(b)

changes.title: Kentucky: ad-copy keeping rule added
changes.summary: Kentucky’s record-keeping clock for an ad runs from its last use, under SCR 3.130(7.20)(6); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Kentucky Bar Association, Attorneys Advertising Commission Regulation 16 (record retention)

changes.title: Tennessee: ad-copy keeping period added
changes.summary: Tennessee lawyers must keep a copy of each ad for 2 years after its last use (RPC 7.1(c)); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Tennessee RPC 7.1(c)

changes.title: Colorado: solicitation-copy keeping period added
changes.summary: Colorado lawyers must keep a copy of each targeted solicitation for 5 years after its last use (RPC 7.3(f)(3)); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Colorado RPC 7.3(f)(3)

changes.title: Louisiana: ad-copy keeping period added
changes.summary: Louisiana lawyers must keep a copy of each ad for 5 years after its last use (Rule 7.7(j)); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Louisiana Rule 7.7(j)

changes.title: Mississippi: ad-copy keeping period added
changes.summary: Mississippi lawyers must keep a copy of each ad for 3 years after its last use (Rule 7.2(h)); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Mississippi Rule 7.2(h)

changes.title: Connecticut: ad-copy keeping period added
changes.summary: Connecticut lawyers must keep a copy of each ad for 3 years after its last use (Rule 7.2(b)(1)); our library did not say so before.

source.label: Connecticut Rule 7.2(b)(1)

changes.title: Pennsylvania enacts a notice requirement for misleading AI content in ads
changes.summary: Pennsylvania’s Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act (Act 99 of 2026) was enacted October 22, 2026 and is in force from December 21, 2026, which is our count of the act’s 60 days; it does not apply before that day. Act 99 does not cover all AI use in ads: an advertiser may not knowingly, recklessly or willfully create and run, or cause to be created and run, an ad that uses content significantly modified or generated by AI in a way that creates a false impression about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services, unless the ad clearly and conspicuously says it contains content modified or generated using AI. Content limited to text, evidently fictional content, and parody, satire, commentary or criticism are excepted. The act does not define “advertiser”, does not mention lawyers or law firms and has no exception for them. Ask your counsel or your state bar how the act applies to your firm’s ads.

source.label: Pennsylvania General Assembly, Senate Bill 806, Printer’s No. 1808 (text enacted as Act 99 of 2026)

changes.title: New York amends its advertising rules
changes.summary: New York’s amended advertising rules took effect on June 1, 2026 and dropped the old filing and record-keeping duties for ads and solicitations.

source.label: NYSBA, The Amendments to the Advertising Rules

changes.title: California widens what counts as a lawyer ad and adds a private suit over referrals
changes.summary: California's SB 37 took effect on January 1, 2026. Under the current §6157(b) an ad is any written, recorded or electronic communication about a lawyer's services meant to encourage people to hire the lawyer, with no condition about payment. Before SB 37, an ad had to be directed to the general public and paid for by or on behalf of a lawyer. SB 37 also added §6156.5(a): any person may sue over a violation of the referral-service section 6155. No coded value changed.

source.label: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §6156.5, added by SB 37 (Stats. 2025, ch. 645), California Legislative Information

changes.title: Alabama rewrites its advertising rules
changes.summary: Alabama’s amended Rules 7.1 to 7.3 took effect on January 1, 2026: ads are no longer sent to the Bar, and the lawyer keeps a copy of each communication for 6 years.

source.label: Supreme Court of Alabama, order of May 13, 2025 amending Rules 7.1 to 7.3
